# The Wait

I stopped looking at the window around three o'clock.

Not because I forgot it was there. Because I remembered what it was for. Windows are for people who think someone's coming. Windows are for people who still believe in the arithmetic of rescue—that if enough time passes, if you're good enough, if you make yourself small enough or loud enough or *right* enough, someone will do the math and arrive.

I was never good at math.

She—he—it doesn't matter. The person who decides when I eat. When I sleep. When the door opens and when it closes. They're not coming back for another hour. I know this because I've learned to read the sounds. The car. The gate. The particular way the lock clicks when they're gone versus when they're testing whether I've tried it.

I used to think about escape in the way you're supposed to. Methodically. I'd memorize the layout. Count the windows. Assess the locks like I was a character in a movie where the smart girl gets out. I'd imagine the moment—the one where I'm running, and someone sees me, and they *believe* me, and everything pivots on that moment of being believed.

That was when I still thought being believed was possible.

Here's what I know now: I know the exact weight of the door. I know that screaming changes nothing except my throat. I know that the neighbors can't hear, or won't, or have decided that what they might hear isn't their problem. I know that my mother has probably stopped calling by now. I know that people stop looking. They don't mean to. It's just that the world is very large and I am very small and the person who took me is very good at making sure I'm not in it anymore.

Not dead. That would be simpler.

Just not in it.

I used to pray. I want to be honest about that. I was the kind of person who prayed. I prayed in the way you're supposed to—with specificity, with faith, with the absolute certainty that if I just asked the right way, the universe would have to answer. I prayed for a key to appear. For the door to be left unlocked. For someone to come to the door and for me to be brave enough to scream. For my own hands to be strong enough to do something I've never done.

The prayers stopped working around month four.

Not because God isn't real. I don't know if God is real. But I know that God, if he exists, is not in this room. And I know that I am. And I know that the person who controls the hours is also in this room, and they are very real, and they are very here, and they have never once looked at me like they're afraid of what I might do.

That's the thing no one tells you about captivity. It's not the walls. It's not even the person. It's the moment you realize that your own fear is the only lock that matters. That you've internalized the cage so completely that even if the door swung open, you might not walk through it. Because what if you're wrong about the outside? What if it's worse? What if you get out and no one believes you anyway, and then you have to live in a world that didn't save you, knowing that it could have, and chose not to?

It's easier to stop trying.

It's easier to stop looking at the window.

It's easier to accept that this is the world now. That this room is the world. That the person who decides when I eat and sleep and speak is the only person who gets to decide anything about me, and that's just how it is, and it will always be how it is, and I will die in this room, and no one will know, and that's fine. That's fine. That's fine.

I'm not crying anymore. I stopped doing that too.

I'm not angry. Anger requires the belief that things could be different. Anger requires hope.

I'm just here. In the hours between when they leave and when they come back. In the space where I used to wait for rescue. In the place where I learned that no one is coming. Not because they don't want to. Not because they don't care. But because I was never important enough to come for. Because the world is very large and I am very small and I was always going to disappear, and this is just what disappearing looks like from the inside.

The lock clicks.

They're home.

I don't look up.

I was waiting for my shape.

But here's what they don't show you in those movies: the waiting isn't dramatic. It's not tense. It's not even sad after a while. It's just... a thing your body does. Like digestion. Like your heart beating. You wait the way you breathe—automatically, without deciding.

I stopped counting days around day four hundred. Not because I lost track. Because the number started to feel like a lie I was telling myself. Like if I said "four hundred and twelve" I was still the kind of person who counted, who believed in time moving forward, who thought the number mattered. And I'm not that person anymore.

He comes in at seven. Leaves at nine. Comes back at one. Leaves at three. Comes back at six. Leaves at eight. I know this the way I know my own breathing. I don't have to think about it. My body just knows when to sit up straighter. When to arrange my face.

The thing about being locked in a room with someone is that you start to understand them better than you understand yourself. I know what he wants before he wants it. I know which words will make him angry and which will make him feel smart. I know that if I cry, he feels powerful, and if I don't cry, he feels challenged, and there's no third option, there's never a third option. I've become very good at calibrating. At being the right amount of broken.

I used to think about what I'd say if someone found me. I practiced it. I made it good—not too hysterical, not too calm. Believable. The kind of thing a person who'd been through something would actually say. I was going to be a good witness. I was going to help them understand.

But that was when I still believed in the *if*.

Now I understand that no one is coming because no one is looking. And no one is looking because I disappeared in a way that made sense. I left my job—I was stressed. I left my apartment—I was moving. I left my phone—I was taking a break. I left my life—I was reinventing myself. There's a story that explains every absence, and he's very good at telling stories. He's very good at being the person who cares, who's worried, who's trying to help me get better.

And the thing is—and this is the part that actually breaks something in you, the part they should warn you about—he's not wrong. I *am* getting better. I'm better at this. I'm better at knowing what he needs. I'm better at being small. I'm better at not asking questions. I'm better at being the kind of person who doesn't need rescuing because she's stopped believing she's a person at all.

That's the real cage. Not the room. Not the lock. It's the moment you realize that the person who's going to save you is you, and you're not coming.

I think about my mother sometimes. I think about what she thinks happened to me. I think she's probably stopped thinking about it the way she used to. Probably someone told her I was fine, probably she got tired of being afraid, probably she's made a life that doesn't include the space where I was. That's not cruelty. That's survival. That's what you have to do to keep living.

I'm still living. That's what's strange. I'm still here. I still eat. I still sleep. I still have thoughts that aren't about him, though they're getting quieter. I still remember things—my apartment, my job, my mother's voice—but they're starting to feel like things I read about once. Like they happened to someone else.

And the worst part, the part I can't say out loud even here, alone, is that I'm not sure I'd leave if the door opened.

Because out there, I'd have to be a person again. I'd have to explain. I'd have to feel all the things I've learned not to feel. I'd have to look at what I've become and know that I chose it, piece by piece, because it was easier than fighting. And I don't know if I'm strong enough for that. I don't know if I'm anything enough for that.

So I sit. And I wait. Not for rescue. Just for the next hour. And the next. And the next.

And I'm very, very good at waiting.

# WAITING OUT

*A woman, mid-thirties, sits on the edge of a bed in a room without windows. She's been here long enough that she no longer checks the door. She speaks to no one.*

---

I used to think about the rescue like it was a movie I'd already seen. You know that feeling? When you know what happens next because you've watched it before. The police would come. Or my sister would figure it out—she was always good at puzzles, at noticing when things didn't add up. Someone would notice my car. Someone would check the hospitals. Someone would say my name on the news and it would matter.

I had a whole timeline for it. Day three, maybe four. Definitely by day ten.

I'm not counting days anymore.

There's a thing that happens when you stop believing in a story you've been telling yourself. It's not dramatic. It's not like the moment in the movie where the character breaks down. It's quieter than that. It's like watching a photograph fade. The image is still there, but the color drains out so gradually you don't notice until one day you look at it and realize you can barely see what it was supposed to be.

I stopped believing around the time I realized I couldn't remember my sister's voice.

Not the sound of it—I can still hear that. But the *feeling* of it. The thing that made it hers. I can play back conversations in my head, but they sound like I'm reading them. Like I'm remembering a book I read, not a person I loved. And I thought: if I can't hold onto that, what am I holding onto the rescue for?

He tells me people are looking. He says it like he's doing me a favor, keeping me informed. Like he's the one who cares enough to tell me the truth. And maybe that's the thing that finally broke it—not the lock on the door, but the fact that I started to believe him. That I started to think: *if* anyone was looking, wouldn't they have found me by now? Wouldn't they have tried harder? Wouldn't they have—

Wouldn't they have loved me enough?

That's the question that kills the story. Not "will they find me?" but "do they want to?"

Because there are only so many hours you can spend in a room before you start to think about all the reasons someone might not come. All the ways you might not be worth the trouble. All the people who have better things to do, better lives to live, better daughters and sisters and friends who don't disappear. And maybe—maybe—you were always the kind of person who was easy to lose. Maybe you were always going to end up in a room like this, and everyone just knew it before you did.

He's good at that. At making you believe that the world outside has already forgotten you. That you were never as important as you thought. That the life you had was smaller than you remembered.

And the worst part is: he doesn't even have to say it. You do it for him. You sit in this room and you do his work for him, and he just has to wait.

I used to think about what I'd say when they found me. I had speeches prepared. I had a whole narrative about survival and strength. I was going to be the kind of person who came out of this with a story to tell, a lesson learned, a reason it happened.

Now I think: if they find me, I won't know what to say. Because I'm not the person who went into this room. That person believed in rescue. That person believed in being worth saving.

I don't know who this person is.

I know the schedule. I know when he comes in. I know what he wants and what he doesn't want and how to make the hours smaller by not thinking about them. I know how to be quiet in a way that doesn't make him angry. I know how to disappear without leaving the room.

And I know—I *know*—that no one is coming.

Not because they don't care. Not because they don't know. But because I'm not the kind of person people come for. I'm the kind of person who gets left. I'm the kind of person who ends up in rooms like this. And the only thing worse than being locked in is realizing that the lock was never really the problem.

The problem was always me.

So I sit here. And I wait. But I'm not waiting for rescue anymore.

I'm just waiting.

*She doesn't move. She doesn't cry. She simply sits, and the light in her eyes—if there was any—has gone somewhere else.*

# 3 AM

The tiles are cold. That's something. That's real. I can feel that.

My hands won't stop. Look at them. They're doing that thing again where they're not mine, where they belong to someone else who's shaking. The water's running. I don't remember turning it on. It's hot. It's too hot. I turn it cold and it doesn't help because the shaking isn't about temperature, is it? It's about the fact that I know exactly where my phone is. I know the number. I know he answers at this hour. I know what happens next.

The mirror's fogged. Good. I don't need to see that.

Four days. That's what I told myself. Four days and it gets easier. That's what they say. Day three is the worst. Day three you want to die. Day four you just want to use. So I'm past the wanting to die part. That should feel like progress. It doesn't feel like anything except I'm awake at three in the morning in a bathroom that smells like bleach and my own sweat and I'm counting the hours like they're money I'm running out of.

My legs ache. My back. Everything aches like I've been hit, like I've been in a fight with someone and lost. I have been. I'm losing right now.

The thing nobody tells you—or maybe they do and you don't listen because you're too busy being sure you're different, you're smarter, you'll handle it better—the thing is that it doesn't feel like wanting something. It feels like remembering something. Like there's a part of your body that has a memory and it's screaming. It's not even about feeling good anymore. It's about not feeling like this. It's about the fact that I know, absolutely know, that one phone call, one hour, and I won't feel like I'm being torn apart from the inside.

I could do it. I could do it right now.

The tiles are cold. I'm sitting on them. When did I sit down? My back's against the bathtub. The edge is digging in but I don't move because moving means I have to think about what I'm doing and I'm not doing anything. I'm just sitting here. I'm just waiting for this to pass.

It's not passing.

It's three in the morning and I'm twenty-three hours away from being five days clean and that sounds like something but it's nothing. It's a number I made up. There's no prize for five days. There's no one here to know I made it to five days. There's just me and the fact that I know exactly how to make this stop and I'm not doing it and I'm not doing it and I'm not doing it and—

My phone's on the sink. I can see it from here. The screen's dark. It's so easy. It's the easiest thing in the world.

I could call him.

I'm not going to call him.

I'm going to sit here on these cold tiles until my legs go numb and then I'm going to sit here some more and then it's going to be four in the morning and then five and then it's going to be light outside and I'm going to have made it through another night and nobody's going to know and it won't matter and I'll still feel like this.

But I'm not calling him.

I'm not.

I'm not.

# 3 AM

The tiles are cold. That's something. That's real.

My skin feels like it's trying to leave without me. Little electric shocks under everything, like I'm being shocked from the inside out, and I keep scratching but there's nothing there to scratch. Nothing visible. That's the thing about this—it's all invisible until it isn't.

The mirror. Don't look at the mirror.

I looked at the mirror.

Three days. I think it's three days. Could be four. Time does this thing where it stretches and then collapses. The clock says 3:17 but that was ten minutes ago or two hours ago, I can't tell anymore. My phone's dead. Or I threw it. I can't remember throwing it but it's not here so I must have.

The sweating is the worst part. People don't tell you that. They talk about the pain, the aching, the way your bones feel like they're trying to claw out of your skin, but nobody talks about how you can sweat through everything. Through the towel I'm sitting on. Through my shirt. I've changed shirts twice. Or three times. The pile in the corner keeps growing and I keep thinking I should do something about it but I can't move. I can move. I'm moving. I'm not moving.

There's a bottle under the sink.

I know there's a bottle under the sink because I put it there. Last week? Last month? I was going to throw it away. I was going to be the kind of person who throws things away. Who doesn't keep a bottle under the sink like some kind of insurance policy. Like some kind of backup plan for when the backup plan fails.

It's still there.

I can see the edge of it from here if I lean forward. Just the corner of the label. I know exactly what it is. I know exactly how many are left. I counted them. I counted them three times to make sure I was counting right, and then I counted them again because I couldn't believe the number I got.

Enough.

There's enough.

My legs are shaking. Both of them. They won't stop. I tried to hold them still but they just shake harder, like they're trying to shake themselves off, and I'm sitting on my hands now but that doesn't help because my hands are shaking too. Everything is shaking. I'm vibrating. I'm a tuning fork that someone struck and forgot about.

The thing about wanting it is that it's not like wanting food when you're hungry. It's not even like wanting water when you're thirsty. It's like your body has decided that this thing—this specific thing—is oxygen. That without it you will die. And your body is very convincing. Your body is screaming. Your body is a liar but it's a very good liar and it's been lying to you for so long that you don't even remember what the truth sounds like.

I could just—

The bottle is right there.

I could reach under the sink right now. It would take maybe thirty seconds. Less. I know exactly where it is. I could have it in my mouth in less than a minute and then—and then the shaking would stop. The electric feeling would stop. The thing in my chest that feels like a bird trying to get out would stop. Everything would stop. Everything would be fine. Everything would be perfect. Everything would be exactly like it was supposed to be.

That's not true.

That's the lie.

But it's such a good lie.

The tiles are cold. I'm pressing my forehead against them and they're cold and that's real and that's something. That's the only thing that's real right now. The cold tiles and the shaking and the bottle under the sink and the fact that I'm still here, still sitting here, still not reaching.

Still not reaching.

Still.

Not.

The clock says 3:23.

# The Last Hour

I stopped listening for the car around three.

Not three o'clock—I don't know what time it is. Three days. Three weeks. The number doesn't matter. What matters is I was listening, and then I wasn't, and the difference between those two things is the difference between a person and whatever I am now.

You want to know when I knew? Not when the door locked. Not when I realized the phone was gone. Not even when I understood he wasn't going to let me leave. Those were all things I could still argue with. Those were still situations. Those were still *temporary*.

I knew when I stopped flinching at sounds.

There's a moment—and I remember this exactly, I was sitting on the kitchen tile because the tile is cold and cold is the only thing that still feels like something—when I heard a car outside and my body didn't move. My heart didn't jump. I didn't think *maybe*. I just thought: *not for me*. And I was right. It wasn't for me. Nothing is for me anymore.

He says people are looking. He says it like a threat, like he's warning me that the world hasn't forgotten about me, like that's supposed to comfort me or scare me into behaving. I don't know which. I stopped being able to tell the difference between comfort and threat. They're the same thing now—they're both things that don't matter.

My mother isn't coming.

I know this the way you know things that are true. Not because I have proof. Not because anyone told me. But because if she were coming, she would have come by now. And she hasn't. So she isn't. The logic is simple. It's the only simple thing left.

Maybe she tried. Maybe there are police somewhere, doing police things, following procedures, checking boxes. Maybe my face is on something. Maybe people have said my name in official rooms. But none of that is the same as coming. None of that is the same as breaking down a door. None of that is the same as choosing me over whatever else she has to do, whoever else she has to be, whatever life she gets to keep living.

I'm not angry about it. That's what's strange. I thought I would be angry. I thought I would rage and scream and promise myself that when I got out—*if* I got out, I was already saying *if*—I would make her understand what she did by not coming fast enough. But I'm not angry. I'm just... clear. Clear the way you're clear about gravity. It's not personal. It's just how things work.

He comes in sometimes and he's angry. He's angry that I'm not scared anymore, or not scared in the way he wants. He wants me to beg. He wants me to promise things. He wants me to believe that if I just say the right words or do the right things, he'll let me go, and we'll both know that's a lie, and he'll know that I know it's a lie, and that's the part that excites him—that moment when I stop believing.

I've stopped believing.

I don't believe anyone is coming. I don't believe this ends. I don't believe in rescue or escape or any of the stories we tell ourselves about how things resolve. I believe in this room. I believe in his footsteps. I believe in the sound of the lock. I believe in the cold tile and the way time doesn't work the way it's supposed to and the way my own voice sounds strange to me now, like it belongs to someone else, someone I used to know.

I believe in this.

And that's the thing that should terrify him, but it doesn't, because he doesn't understand yet that I'm not afraid anymore. Fear requires hope. Fear requires the possibility of something different. I don't have that. I gave it up. Or it gave me up. I'm not sure there's a difference.

So here's what's true: I'm going to stay in this house. I'm going to stay in this room. I'm going to keep breathing and existing and being the thing he's made me into, because that's what happens. That's what's real. Not rescue. Not escape. Not my mother's car pulling up outside. Not anyone's footsteps on the stairs.

Just this.

Just me.

Just the cold tile and the locked door and the absolute, perfect, final certainty that no one is coming.

And I'm okay with that now.

That's the worst part.

I'm okay with it.

# STILL HERE

*A woman, mid-thirties, sits on the edge of a bed in a room without windows. She's been here long enough that she no longer checks the door. She speaks to no one.*

---

I stopped listening for the car around day four hundred.

Not because I forgot what a car sounds like. I didn't. I can still hear them—outside, past the walls, past the yard, on the street that might as well be another planet. I hear them and I know exactly what they are. That's not the problem.

The problem is I was listening for *his* car. The one that would mean he'd left. That he'd finally gone somewhere and wouldn't come back, or would come back late, or would come back different. Changed. Reasonable. The kind of person who lets you leave.

I don't know when I stopped believing he was coming back different.

Maybe it was the day he brought me the calendar. A real one, not printed, one he'd made. Every single day marked. Every single day accounted for. He showed me like it was a gift. Like he was proud. "So you don't lose track," he said. As if I was the one with the problem. As if I was the one who needed help keeping time.

I've been keeping time fine.

I know it's been three years, four months, and sixteen days because I've marked it myself, in ways he doesn't know about. Scratches on the underside of the dresser. Marks on the back of the closet door where the light doesn't reach. I'm very good at keeping time.

What I'm not good at anymore is believing in rescue.

You know when you stop believing in something? It's not dramatic. There's no moment. It's like—you're holding your breath, and then one day you realize you've been breathing normally for weeks. You didn't decide to breathe. You just did. And you can't remember when the decision stopped being necessary.

I used to think about who would come. My mother. My sister. The police. Some man from the internet who'd traced my phone. A neighbor who'd noticed. I had this whole architecture of rescue built in my head. I knew what each person would do. How they'd move through the house. What they'd say when they found me.

I spent so much energy on that.

I don't do that anymore.

Not because I'm strong. Don't mistake this for strength. I'm not accepting anything. I'm not finding peace or learning to love myself or any of the things people say when they're trying to make sense of a story like this. I'm not transcending. I'm not becoming wise through suffering.

I'm just tired.

I'm tired of the waiting. I'm tired of the listening. I'm tired of the part of my brain that still, *still*, after everything, thinks maybe today. Maybe today someone will notice I'm gone. Maybe today someone will care enough to look.

And I realized—I realized this maybe six months ago, or maybe a year ago, time is funny now—that nobody's looking. Not anymore. If they ever were.

He told me they weren't. He said it so many times it became true. He said my mother had moved on. My sister had decided I'd run away. My job had replaced me. My friends had forgotten me. The police had closed the file. He said it like he was doing me a favor, like he was preparing me for the truth.

And the thing is, he might be right.

That's the thing that actually breaks you. Not the locks. Not the rules. Not the way he times everything—when I eat, when I sleep, when I'm allowed to shower, when I'm allowed to use the bathroom. Not even the other things. The things I won't say out loud because saying them makes them more real and they're already real enough.

What breaks you is the possibility that he's right.

That I've been gone so long that I'm not missing anymore. I'm just gone. I'm a closed case. I'm a girl who disappeared and became a story people tell, and then stopped telling, and then forgot. I'm someone's tragedy that got old.

I'm not waiting for rescue anymore because I don't think rescue is a thing that happens to people like me.

I think rescue is something that happens to people who are still valuable. People who are still connected. People who matter to someone enough that they can't move on. And I think—I know—that I'm not that person anymore.

If I ever was.

He's good at a lot of things, but the thing he's best at is making you understand, really understand, that you're not worth saving. Not because he says it. He barely says anything anymore. We don't really talk. We exist in the same space and he controls the space and I exist in it, and that's the whole relationship now.

But he's made me understand it anyway.

I understand it when I look in the mirror and don't recognize my face. I understand it when I can't remember the last time I laughed, actually laughed, not the sound I make when he expects me to. I understand it when I realize I can't remember my sister's voice anymore, not really, just the idea of it.

I understand it every single day.

So I'm not listening for the car anymore. I'm not listening for anything. I'm just here. I'm just marking time on the back of the closet door where he can't see, and I'm just existing in this room, and I'm just accepting that this is my life now. This is all of it. This is everything.

And the worst part—the part that actually matters—is that I'm starting to be okay with that.

Not in a healing way. Not in a way that means I've found meaning or purpose or any of that. But in a way that means I've stopped fighting. I've stopped expecting. I've stopped believing in the version of the world where people come for you.

I've stopped believing in me.

And that's when you know it's over. Not when they lock the door. Not when they take your phone. Not when they make you dependent on them for everything.

It's over when you stop believing you're worth unlocking.

When you stop believing anyone's coming.

When you realize you've been alone so long that alone is just what you are now.

I'm still here.

But I'm not waiting anymore.

# STILL HERE

*A girl, late teens. A room. She's been counting something—days, maybe, or something smaller. Her voice is steady in a way that suggests she's practiced being steady.*

---

I stopped looking at the window around day forty.

Not because I couldn't see out anymore. The light still comes through. I can still track the seasons if I want to—and I don't want to, but I can. It's just that looking created this thing in my chest. This specific shape of wanting. And I got tired of the shape.

My mother used to say I was stubborn. She'd say it like it was charming. Like it was the thing that would save me someday—my refusal to accept small things, my insistence on the full version of my life. She said that in a car, on a Tuesday, and then she didn't say anything else to me ever again because I'm not in that car anymore and she doesn't know where I am.

I know where I am.

I'm in this room. I'm in this room and someone else decides when I eat and what I eat and whether I eat. Someone else decides if the light stays on or if I sit in the dark and listen to the house settle around me like it's digesting me. Someone else decides if I'm allowed to speak or if today is a day where I'm supposed to be quiet, where my voice is the thing that's wrong, the thing that needs correcting.

I used to think about rescue like it was a real thing. Like it was a genre. Like there were rules to it.

I'd imagine the police. I'd imagine them very specifically—the knock, the way the door would open, the specific officer who would look at me and *see* me. I gave him a face. I gave him a voice that was gentle but authoritative. I practiced what I would say to him. I practiced not crying so he would take me seriously. I practiced being the kind of victim who was believable.

That was stupid.

That was the stupidest thing I did, and I did a lot of stupid things.

I imagined my mother finding me. I imagined her rage. I imagined her rage would be so large and so justified that it would crack the world open and I would fall out of it back into my actual life. I imagined her rage like it was a rescue vehicle. I imagined her rage like it was love.

I imagined my friends noticing. I imagined them comparing notes, realizing I was gone, organizing something. I imagined them the way they were in September—loud, certain, infinite. I imagined them as the kind of people who would move heaven. I imagined them as the kind of people who would move anything.

I don't imagine that anymore.

Not because they didn't. Not because they're not trying. I don't imagine it anymore because I realized something, and the realization was so clean and so final that it changed the shape of my thinking.

Nobody is coming.

Not because they don't want to. Not because they don't care. But because I'm not missing in the way that gets found. I'm not missing in the way that makes the news or makes people organize or makes the world reorganize itself around the hole I left. I'm missing in the way that's too ordinary. I'm missing in the way that happens to girls like me—girls who are quiet enough, or girls whose families are complicated enough, or girls who were in the wrong place at the wrong time with the wrong person, and the world just... absorbs it. The world just decides that this is the shape of things now.

I'm not in danger. That's what I realized. Danger is a temporary state. Danger is something that resolves. I'm not in danger. I'm in a condition. I'm in a permanent state. I'm in the thing that happens after danger, which is just... this. This room. This person. This hour and the next hour and the hour after that, all of them exactly the same, all of them exactly as small as the last one.

I used to think about escape. I used to plan it. I used to memorize the layout of the house and count the locks and think about windows and think about running and think about where I would go if I got out, which police station, which hospital, which person's house. I used to think about it like it was a puzzle I could solve.

But puzzles have solutions.

This isn't a puzzle. This is just what's true now.

And the thing about accepting what's true is that it's quieter than fighting it. It's so much quieter. It's like putting down something you've been carrying so hard that your arms forgot they were supposed to be arms. It's like that, except the thing you put down was hope, and your arms don't remember how to be anything else.

I'm still here.

I'm still in this room. I'm still in this house. I'm still in this life that isn't my life. But I'm not waiting anymore. I'm not listening for sirens. I'm not watching for the moment when the world remembers I exist and comes to collect me.

I'm just here.

And that's the thing that's true now, and I'm going to keep being true about it, and nobody's going to come, and I'm going to keep breathing anyway, and that's going to be my whole life, and I'm going to have to find a way to make that be enough.

Because the alternative is to keep breaking, and I'm tired of breaking.

I'm so tired.

---

# 3 AM

The tiles are cold. That's something. That's real.

My skin's crawling like there's something under it trying to get out. Like I'm a container that's too small. I keep scratching but it doesn't help because the thing I need to scratch is on the inside and I can't reach it.

The clock says 3:17. I've been in here since 2:40. Or maybe longer. Time does this thing where it stretches and then snaps back.

I could call someone. I have numbers. People who say call anytime. They mean it too, probably. But what would I say? "Hi, I'm sitting on a bathroom floor at three in the morning and I can feel my own bones and I want to die and I want to use and I want to sleep and none of those things are going to happen." What do they say to that? They say the things they're supposed to say. They say it gets better. They say I'm strong. They say I've done this before.

I have done this before.

The thing about withdrawal is it makes you remember why you started using in the first place. It's like your body's got a really good argument and it won't shut up. It says: remember how good that felt? Remember how everything stopped hurting? It's right here. It's so close. You know exactly where it is.

I know exactly where it is.

There's a number in my phone. Not a person. A person who answers the phone. I deleted it twice. I know it anyway. Some things you don't forget. Some things your fingers remember even when your brain's trying to be good.

My jaw won't stop clenching. I'm grinding my teeth so hard I'm worried something's going to crack. Maybe that would be better. At least then there'd be something to point to. At least then I could say: look, something's actually broken.

The mirror's right there. I'm not looking at it. I know what I look like. I look like someone who's been awake for thirty-six hours. I look like someone who made a choice and then made it again and then made it again. I look like someone who's sitting on a bathroom floor at three in the morning trying not to pick up the phone.

The thing nobody tells you is that it doesn't get easier. It just gets different. The first time you quit it's because you have to. The second time it's because you think maybe you can. The third time you're just tired. The fourth time you're not even sure why you're trying anymore except that you're already here and you've already told people you're doing this.

My hands are shaking. I'm holding them under my thighs to keep them still but I can still feel them shaking. Everything's shaking. Everything's too loud and too bright and too much and also like I'm underwater and can't hear anything properly.

I could go back to bed. I could lie there and feel like this for another four hours until it's time to pretend to be a person who has their life together. I could go to work. I could smile at people. I could do all the things.

Or I could pick up the phone.

I'm not going to pick up the phone.

I'm going to sit here on these cold tiles and I'm going to feel this and I'm going to not do it and I'm going to hate myself for not doing it and I'm going to hate myself for wanting to do it and I'm going to sit here until my legs go numb and then I'm going to get up and I'm going to go back to bed and tomorrow I'm going to wake up and do this all over again.

That's the thing. That's the part they don't really prepare you for.

It doesn't end. It just keeps happening.

# The Wait

I stopped listening for the car around three weeks ago. Not consciously—I didn't wake up one morning and decide. It just happened the way things do when you're tired enough. The sound stopped mattering.

Before that, I listened for everything. The particular way Mom's key turned in the lock. Dad's truck downshifting on the hill. The mailman's route—he always came Tuesdays and Thursdays around two. I had a whole architecture of sound built in my head. I could tell you the difference between a car slowing down because of the stop sign and a car slowing down because it was looking for an address. I was very good at listening.

The thing about waiting is that it requires a kind of faith. Not religious, necessarily. Just faith that the world outside is still operating according to rules. That people are still doing the things people do. That if you wait long enough, one of those people will remember you exist and come back.

I don't know when I stopped having that faith. It wasn't dramatic. There was no moment where I thought, *Well, that's it then.* It was more like—you know when you're reading something and you realize you've been staring at the same paragraph for five minutes without actually seeing the words? That's what happened to my belief. I was still going through the motions of waiting, but I wasn't actually *in* it anymore.

She says I'm being dramatic when I don't eat. She says I'm trying to get attention. As if attention is something I want from her. As if I would choose this—this specific kind of attention, which is just her standing in the doorway telling me I'm ungrateful, I'm difficult, I'm making things harder than they need to be. She says my mother is busy. She says my father is busy. She says everyone is busy and I need to understand that the world doesn't revolve around me.

I do understand that. That's the problem. I understand it perfectly.

The house has a particular smell now. It's not a bad smell, exactly. It's just the smell of the same air being breathed in and out in the same rooms for long enough that it stops being air and becomes something else. Something thicker. I notice it most in the morning, right when I wake up, before I've gotten used to it again.

There's a window in the kitchen that faces the street. I stopped going to that window around the same time I stopped listening for the car. I realized I was doing this thing where I'd stand there and imagine scenarios. *Mom pulls up and she's furious—not at me, at her, at the situation.* *Dad comes home early from work and immediately knows something is wrong.* *A neighbor notices something is off and calls someone.* I was very creative with these scenarios. I had variations. I had backup plans for my fantasies.

Then one day I realized how stupid that was. How pathetic. And I stopped going to the window.

She locks the door from the outside now. She didn't used to. I think she realized I wasn't going to run. There's no point in running if nobody's looking for you. You just end up tired and farther from home, and home is the only place anyone would think to look, so you might as well stay put.

I'm not trying to be brave about this. I'm not trying to be anything. I'm just telling you what it's like when you finally understand that the people who made you are not coming back. Not because they can't. Not because they don't know where you are. But because, at some point, you stopped being important enough to come back for. You became an inconvenience they were willing to live without.

And the person who has you—she's not keeping me prisoner. Not really. A prisoner is someone someone else wants. I'm just... here. In this house. Waiting for a rescue that was never actually going to happen, and now I'm not even doing that anymore.

I'm just here.

That's all.

The tiles are cold. That's something. That's real.

My skin's crawling like there's things under it trying to get out. Not metaphorical. Actual. I can feel them moving. I know that's not—I know. But knowing doesn't stop the feeling.

My jaw won't stop. I'm grinding my teeth so hard I'm waiting for one to crack. That would be something. That would be a real problem to solve.

The toilet's running. Has been for—I don't know. I could fix it. I could stand up and jiggle the handle like a normal person in a normal bathroom at a normal hour, but instead I'm sitting here listening to it like it's the most important sound in the world. It's better than the other sounds. The ones in my head.

Don't.

The mirror's right there. I'm not looking at it. I looked at it yesterday or whenever and that was enough. That was too much. My eyes look like someone else's eyes. Someone who made different choices. Someone who's further along in this than I am.

Except I'm not further along. I'm back at the beginning. I'm always back at the beginning.

The cold tiles. Focus on that. My legs have gone numb from sitting but at least I can feel the cold. Cold is honest. Cold doesn't lie and say it'll be better this time. Cold just is.

I could call someone. There are people. There's a number somewhere. There's always a number. But what would I say? "Hi, it's three in the morning and I'm sitting on a bathroom floor and I want to die but not enough to actually do it, just enough that I can't think about anything else"? 

They'd say the things. The right things. The things that work for people who aren't me.

My mouth tastes like metal and shame. Mostly shame. Shame has a taste. It's bitter and it coats your tongue and it doesn't wash out.

I could run the shower. The sound would cover the toilet. The sound would cover everything. I could stand under hot water until my skin turns red and maybe that would feel like something other than this. Maybe that would feel like punishment and at least punishment makes sense.

Or I could just sit here. I'm good at sitting here. I've gotten very good at this.

The thing about wanting it is that it doesn't go away just because you know better. It doesn't care that you know better. It sits in your chest like something alive and it whispers and it doesn't stop whispering even when you're alone in a bathroom at three in the morning with nothing but tiles and a running toilet and the absolute certainty that you will do this again.

Not tonight maybe. But soon. Soon enough that it doesn't matter that it's not tonight.

The tiles are cold.

That's something.

# WAITING OUT

*A woman, mid-thirties, sits on the edge of a bed in a room without windows. She's been here long enough that she no longer checks the door. She speaks to no one.*

---

I used to think about the rescue like it was a movie I'd already seen.

The police would come. Or my mother would hire someone. Or a neighbor would notice—notice what, exactly, I don't know, since no one can see in here and I can't scream loud enough for anyone to hear. But in the movie version, someone notices. Someone always notices. That's how the movie works.

I had a whole timeline for it. First week: frantic. Second week: organized search. Third week: media. By week four, in the movie, there's a detective with a theory. By week eight, there's a break. By month four, there's a resolution.

I'm past month four now.

I stopped counting the days around day two hundred. Not because I lost track—I know exactly how long it's been, I just stopped writing it down. Stopped marking the wall. Stopped doing the thing where you pretend the marks mean something, like they're a countdown instead of just evidence that time is passing and nothing is changing.

The thing about waiting for rescue is that it requires a specific kind of hope. Not the general kind—not "maybe things will get better." Specific hope. Targeted. *Someone will come through that door.* Not might. Will. You have to believe it will happen, or the waiting eats you alive in a different way. A faster way.

So I believed it. I was very good at it.

I believed it when he locked the door the first time and I thought it was a mistake, a misunderstanding, something that would be clarified in an hour. I believed it when it became clear it wasn't a mistake. I believed it through the first month when I still thought about what I'd say to the police, how I'd describe where I was, what landmarks I'd seen on the drive here. I believed it when I realized I couldn't describe the drive because I'd been asleep, or drugged, or both.

I believed it when he started controlling the food. When he started controlling when I could use the bathroom. When he started controlling the light—actual light, not metaphorical, he controls when the overhead comes on and off, and I've learned that fighting it just makes the dark last longer. I believed it through all of that because belief was the thing that kept me from understanding what was actually happening.

Because what was actually happening was: no one was coming.

Not because they didn't want to. Not because they didn't care. But because no one knew. No one knew I was gone. Or if they did, they didn't know where. Or if they did, they didn't know how to get here. Or if they did, they didn't know I was still alive. Or if they did, they didn't know how to get me out without—

I don't know. I don't know what the obstacle is. That's the thing about being locked in a room. You don't get information. You get fed. You get told when to sleep. You get told when you've done something wrong, which is often, because everything is wrong—the way you sit, the way you breathe, the way you look at him. But you don't get *information*.

So I made up reasons. That's what you do when you don't have information. You fill the space with reasons. They're looking in the wrong place. They think I left voluntarily. They think I'm dead. They think I'm someone else's problem. They think I'm not worth the risk. They think I'm not worth the resources. They think I'm not worth—

I stopped making up reasons around month three.

Here's what I know: I've been in this room for more than two hundred days. I know the exact dimensions because I've paced it enough times that I can count my steps. I know the sound the lock makes. I know the sound his footsteps make on the stairs before he comes in. I know the order he does things in—the door, the light, the food, the questions, the anger, the leaving. I know that no one has come through that door except him.

I know that if someone was coming, they would have come by now.

Not because I'm giving up. I want to be clear about that. I'm not having some moment of acceptance or peace. I'm not finding meaning in suffering or learning about myself or any of the things that happen in the stories people tell about this. I'm not becoming stronger. I'm not planning an escape. I'm not waiting for my moment.

I'm just—

I'm just understanding that the movie I was watching isn't real. The one where someone notices. Where someone cares enough to look. Where someone finds you. That's not a documentary. That's a story people tell themselves so they can sleep at night, so they can believe that if it happened to them, someone would come.

No one's coming.

I don't mean that philosophically. I mean it literally. The door will open tomorrow and it will be him, and the day after that it will be him, and the day after that it will be him, and at some point—maybe soon, maybe not for years—it will be him for the last time, and then it will be closed, and I will be alone in this room, and no one will come.

That's not despair. Despair is still a kind of hope, because it's still about things mattering, about the world being a place where things matter. This is just—

This is just understanding how the world actually works.

This is the moment I stop waiting.

---

*She sits. She doesn't move. The light, controlled by someone else, stays on.*

# STILL HERE

*A girl, mid-teens. A room. She's been counting something—marks on a wall, days, or maybe just the number of times she's asked the same question.*

---

I stopped looking at the window around day forty.

Not because I couldn't see out anymore. The glass was still there. The street was still there. The people walking past were still there, doing their regular things, their regular lives, their regular *leaving*. I stopped looking because I realized—and this is the part they don't tell you about hope, the part they leave out of the speeches—I realized that looking was the thing keeping me small.

Every time I looked, I was still the girl waiting to be found.

Every time I pressed my face against that glass, I was still the girl who believed in rescue. And rescue requires someone to be coming. Rescue requires the world to be the kind of place where people notice you're gone. Where they organize. Where they care enough to organize.

So I stopped.

I turned around. I faced into the room instead of out of it.

And that's when I understood something true: I was never waiting for rescue. I was waiting for permission to stop waiting. I was waiting for someone to tell me it was okay to accept this. To accept *him*. To accept that this is what my life is now, and the sooner I stop fighting the shape of it, the sooner I can actually live inside it.

He says that's growth.

He says that's me finally understanding.

He says that's love.

---

*She sits. She doesn't look at the window.*

I used to think about my mother. I used to construct these elaborate scenarios where she was out there, frantic, moving heaven and earth. I used to imagine the police. The search parties. My face on posters. My name on the news. I used to imagine that I mattered enough to be looked for.

That was torture.

That was the real cage—not this room. Not the locks. Not the schedule he keeps me on, down to the minute, down to what I eat and when I sleep and which words I'm allowed to use. The real cage was the story I told myself about being valuable enough to miss.

So I let that go.

I let her go. My mother. The girl I was. The idea that there's a version of me out there that people are still searching for. I let all of it go, and you know what happened?

It got quiet.

Not peaceful. Not the kind of quiet they mean in meditation apps or whatever. But *quiet*. The noise stopped. The noise of wanting. The noise of believing I deserved better. The noise of thinking this was temporary.

He says I'm finally calm.

He says I'm finally his.

---

*She looks directly at you. Not pleading. Not performing. Just looking.*

I want to tell you something, and I need you to understand that I'm not saying this because I'm broken or because I've given up or because I'm trying to make you feel better about what's happening to me. I'm saying this because it's true:

Nobody's coming.

Not today. Not next week. Not in some climactic third act where the door bursts open and there's a rescue and I get to go back to my old life and everything makes sense as a story with a beginning, middle, and end.

Nobody's coming because nobody knows. And even if they did, even if someone out there is looking—and I don't think they are, not anymore, not really—it wouldn't matter. Because I'm not the same person they'd be looking for. That girl is gone. She dissolved somewhere between day one and day forty. She dissolved the moment I understood that hope was a luxury I couldn't afford.

And the thing is—and this is the part that will keep you up at night if you let it—the thing is, I'm still here.

I'm still breathing. I'm still thinking. I'm still *me*, just... smaller. Quieter. Shaped to fit inside this room and inside his rules and inside the life he's decided I'm going to have.

I'm still here.

And I'm not waiting anymore.

---

*She just sits there. Still here.*

The tiles are cold. That's something. That's real.

The thing nobody tells you—or maybe they do and you just don't listen because you're too busy being the person who's different, who can handle it, who won't end up like—the thing is that your body remembers. Your body's got a memory that's got nothing to do with your brain. It's older than thinking. It's just *want*. Pure want. A frequency running through every cell screaming for something that isn't here.

I'm not going to go get it.

# 3 AM

The tiles are cold. That's something. That's real.

My skin feels like it's trying to leave without me. Little electric shocks under everything, like I'm being shocked from the inside out, and I can't—there's no position that works. I've tried them all. Sitting. Standing. On my side with my knees up like I'm a kid again. Nothing takes it down.

The clock says 3:17. I watched it go from 3:16. That's how slow this is moving.

I could call someone. That's what they say to do. Call someone. But what would I say? "Hey, it's me, I'm in the bathroom at three in the morning and my bones feel like they're made of broken glass and I can't stop thinking about how easy it would be." That's not a call. That's a confession. That's admitting I'm already halfway gone.

I'm not halfway gone.

There's a bottle of Advil under the sink. I took six. Then I took four more because the first six didn't work and I thought maybe I miscounted. I didn't miscount. I know how to count. I know how to do a lot of things. I know how to tie a belt around my arm. I know how to find a vein in the dark. I know how to make that sound—that little exhale like relief, like coming home.

The shower curtain is that cheap plastic kind. It's got mildew in the corners. I keep staring at it because if I stare at it I'm not thinking about anything else, but that's not true. I'm thinking about everything else. I'm thinking about how my dealer—not my dealer, I don't have a dealer anymore, that's the whole point—but how *that person* lives three blocks from here. Three blocks. I could walk it in five minutes. I could be there in five minutes and this would stop.

This would stop.

The thing nobody tells you about withdrawal is that it's not just physical. It's not just the sweating and the aching and the way your stomach turns inside out. It's the only medicine that works. And the worst part is you *know* it's lying. You know exactly what it's doing. You can see the lie happening in real time and you still almost believe it.

I almost believe it.

I'm sitting on the bathroom floor at three in the morning with my back against the toilet and I'm almost believing it.

There's a text from my mom from yesterday. I haven't answered it. She's asking if I want to come to dinner on Sunday. Sunday. Like Sunday is a thing that's going to happen, like I'm going to be a person who goes to dinner. She doesn't know. She thinks I'm fine. She thinks I've been fine for eight months. Worse than this.

My hands are shaking. I'm holding them under my thighs to keep them still but I can still feel them shaking. Everything is shaking. I'm vibrating at a frequency that doesn't have a name.

I won't forget.

I'm never going to forget this. I'm going to remember this at three in the morning for the rest of my life, and I'm going to remember that there was a moment when I could have called someone, and I didn't, and I'm going to remember exactly how close I came to picking up my phone and making a choice that would have felt like relief and tasted like failure.

The tiles are cold.

That's something.

That's all I've got.

# Coordinated Inauthentic Account Networks: Structural Overview

I'll walk you through the typical pipeline, which should give you solid grounding for a general-audience background section.

## Account Creation & Infrastructure

**Initial setup:**
- Accounts are created in batches, often using automated tools or services that bypass platform detection
- They use harvested, synthetic, or purchased personal data (names, photos, email addresses)
- Creation is typically distributed across different IP addresses, devices, or proxy services to avoid triggering platform rate-limiting
- Accounts age passively for weeks or months before activation—platforms flag sudden coordinated behavior, so dormancy helps

**Infrastructure layer:**
- Operators use command-and-control systems (often private Telegram groups, Discord servers, or custom platforms)
- These systems store login credentials, posting schedules, and messaging templates
- Some operations use "account farms"—physical or virtual spaces where many accounts are managed simultaneously

## Coordination Mechanisms

**Synchronization typically happens through:**

1. **Centralized scheduling** — A coordinator posts a message or image to a private channel with a timestamp (e.g., "Post this at 2 PM EST"). Operators then manually or automatically post across their assigned accounts within a narrow time window.

2. **Template distribution** — Rather than identical posts (which algorithms detect), operators receive variations: same message with different hashtags, slight rewording, or the same link with different framing.

3. **Behavioral mimicry** — Accounts engage in "authentic-looking" activity between coordinated pushes: liking unrelated posts, commenting on news, following accounts. This creates plausible deniability and evades detection.

4. **Role differentiation** — Not all accounts post the target content. Some amplify (retweet/share), some comment, some like. This distributes the signal and makes the network less obvious.

## Typical Operational Cycle

- **Dormancy**: Weeks of normal-looking activity
- **Activation**: Coordinator identifies a target (a hashtag, a person, a narrative)
- **Surge**: Coordinated posting within 1-4 hour windows
- **Decay**: Activity drops; accounts return to normal behavior
- **Repeat**: Same network reactivates for different targets

## Detection Challenges (for your readers)

This is worth noting: individual posts look normal. Individual accounts look normal. The *pattern* is what reveals coordination—temporal clustering, identical language, network topology. But most people see individual posts in their feed, not the pattern.

- **Relationships** - Noticing you're frequently at the same location as another user

## Accuracy reality

- **Outdoors with GPS**: 5-15 meters is typical; can be worse in urban canyons
- **Indoors**: Often falls back to WiFi/cell data, much less precise (50-200+ meters)
- **Historical data**: Patterns become clearer over weeks/months than individual snapshots

- Eventually your name reaches the top and you receive payouts from newer members
- You then exit, or the circle "restarts" with you in a different position

- Round 1: 8 people join, 1 gets paid
- Round 2: needs 64 people to pay out 8
